subject: Should occupancy models default to having random effects on detection?

messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Should occupancy models default to having random effects on detection?
parts:
Hi all,

Repeat measures in a variety of models are handled with random effects. In occupancy models, we assume the occupancy state is fixed throughout the study period and multiple surveys are conducted for each site. Therefore, should the default occupancy model account for the repeat sampling of sites? That is, should the intercepts-only occupancy model:

z_i ~ Bernoulli(psi)
y_ij ~ Bernoulli(z_i * p)

by default be modeled as follows?

z_i ~ Bernoulli(psi)
y_ij ~ Bernoulli(z_i * p_i)
logit(p_i) ~ Normal(mu, sigma)

Cheers,

Matt

messages.author: a4c5d7d1c977b688
messages.subject: Re: Should occupancy models default to having random effects on detection?
parts:
Hi Matthijs (and group),

I would tend to say no if the "default model" means the simplest form of the model. Remember that Bernoulli is already a stochastic process that allows y_ij to vary across j given the same z_i. In that sense there is already a random effect.

Best,
Qing

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: Should occupancy models default to having random effects on detection?
parts:
hi Matt,
 of course this is a reasonable idea because in practice you won't know the true covariates that affect p and so given that you must be missing something this probably shows up as heterogeneity in p. An interesting feature of these sorts of models is that heterogeneity in p can "look like" false positive detections (lots of Discussion in the Royle and Link paper cited below) -- you can't really distinguish those processes from one another with simple occupancy data. Thats tangential to your point though. In summary, p ~ random effect is probably a sensible model but due to the mathematical structure of the model there are some nuances related to identifiability and robustness (I guess those always apply lol).
regards
andy


Royle, J.A., 2006. Site occupancy models with heterogeneous detection probabilities. Biometrics, 62(1), pp.97-102.
Royle, J.A. and Link, W.A., 2006. Generalized site occupancy models allowing for false positive and false negative errors. Ecology, 87(4), pp.835-841.

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: Should occupancy models default to having random effects on detection?
parts:
Dear Matt, all,

first, I feel strongly that the model without additional random effects in the linear predictor for p should be our default. This is dictated by that most important modeling rule of Occam's razor (something like "make things as simple as possible but not simpler"). But I agree that very often, this simple model structure will not be good enough. Accounting for extra dispersion by adding that random effect in p then is what I have often done myself.

Second, I would argue that the z's are clearly random effects: incompletely known quantities that are given a distribution, with shared hyperparameters that we estimate. In the context of a model for latent presence/absence these are the unit-specific unknowns, only they are binary. In contrast, in traditional repeated measures analyses, the unit-specific unknowns are metric-scaled quantities for which normal distributions are adopted.

I would say that the concept of "pooling" would denote the case where every site has the same value of that unit-specific effect z. This does not make sense and so I don't think the pooling concept is helpful in the case of an occupancy model.

Best regards --- Marc

messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Re: Should occupancy models default to having random effects on detection?
parts:
Hey Marc,

Re: your second point, consider the situation where sites are known to be occupied, thereby removing psi and z from the model. Now, y ~ Bernoulli( p), but each site is surveyed more than once. Ignoring the repeated measures here by omitting the site-specific contribution to be p seems to require a justification as opposed to the scenario where the repeated measures are accounted for with a random effect. I don't think anything is fundamentally changed by adding z and psi into the model. I think the repeated meaures in the observation component should be accounted for, no?

Cheers,

Matt

for estimates of psi. Especially if the species has low p overall,
adding random variation to p can lead to substantial positive bias in
occupancy estimates.

Ignoring the repeated measures here by omitting the site-specific contribution to be p seems to require a justification as opposed to the scenario where the repeated measures are accounted for with a random effect. I don't think anything is fundamentally changed by adding z and psi into the model. I think the repeated meaures in the observation component should be accounted for, no?
>
> Cheers,
>
> Matt
>
> On Thursday, January 9, 2025 at 8:21:36 PM UTC+11 marc.kery wrote:
>
> Dear Matt, all,
>
> first, I feel strongly that the model without additional random effects in the linear predictor for p should be our default. This is dictated by that most important modeling rule of Occam's razor (something like "make things as simple as possible but not simpler"). But I agree that very often, this simple model structure will not be good enough. Accounting for extra dispersion by adding that random effect in p then is what I have often done myself.
>
> Second, I would argue that the z's are clearly random effects: incompletely known quantities that are given a distribution, with shared hyperparameters that we estimate. In the context of a model for latent presence/absence these are the unit-specific unknowns, only they are binary. In contrast, in traditional repeated measures analyses, the unit-specific unknowns are metric-scaled quantities for which normal distributions are adopted.
>
> I would say that the concept of "pooling" would denote the case where every site has the same value of that unit-specific effect z. This does not make sense and so I don't think the pooling concept is helpful in the case of an occupancy model.
>
> Best regards --- Marc
>

> Subject: Re: Should occupancy models default to having random effects on detection?
>
> Hey Andy, HNY. I think even with covariates there's a case to be made for including the random site effect on detection simply due to the repeated measures component.
>
> On Thursday, January 9, 2025 at 11:13:10 AM UTC+11 jaroyle wrote:
>
> hi Matt,
> of course this is a reasonable idea because in practice you won't know the true covariates that affect p and so given that you must be missing something this probably shows up as heterogeneity in p. An interesting feature of these sorts of models is that heterogeneity in p can "look like" false positive detections (lots of Discussion in the Royle and Link paper cited below) -- you can't really distinguish those processes from one another with simple occupancy data. >
> z_i ~ Bernoulli(psi)

>
> z_i ~ Bernoulli(psi)

messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Re: Should occupancy models default to having random effects on detection?
parts:
Hey Marc,

Do you mean site-level random effects on detection, on survey-level random effects? When you say "really have to"—would you also omit repeated measures random effects in other models?

Rahel, I ran 1000 simulations for occupancy models with 100 sites, 3, surveys, and Uniform(0, 1) priors for psi and p, with and without site-level random effects on p. Both seem to suffer from the same negative bias in occupancy probability with low p (see attached). Do you have a reference for your claim? It's always possible I made an error in my hasty simulations.

Cheers,

Matt

On Friday, January 10, 2025 at 2:31:41 AM UTC+11 rasrage2 wrote:
Dear all,
I would add that random effects on p can have unintended consequences
for estimates of psi. Especially if the species has low p overall,
adding random variation to p can lead to substantial positive bias in
occupancy estimates.
Best
Rahel

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: Should occupancy models default to having random effects on detection?
parts:
Dear Matt,

ha, you got me there ... no, normally I'd specify those random effects which I think belong into a modeling problem. So, in the simpler model that you sketch, where we have z=1 for all sites (e.g., because we choose to analyse only sites where we know the species occurs), a model with random intercepts in detection would probably be my starting model. And yet, in the more complex site-occupancy model, I think I could not get used to using the analogous model for detection as a start.

I feel that like so many things in modeling, the choice of what we treat as random parameters is to some degree arbitrary. It will in part depend on the richness of your data and on your scientific or management questions. As an example, imagine a GLMM for modeling apparent abundance from some site-year-indexed counts, and with some site-level and some observational-level covariates. In this situation, I would typically specify random intercepts only (and perhaps also model temporal autocorrelation), but I would treat the coefficients of all covariates as fixed, unless I have strong reason against such a choice.

But let's think about these covariates: is it really sensible to assume their effect remains the same over time ? For instance, if these are counts of snakes and my site covariate is a measure of vegetation density. Whether the snakes are more or less visible with a given vegetation density will depend on the temperature: with higher temperature, they will tend to stay more hidden in the vegetation and thus be less visible (to avoid predation), thus decreasing the average count. Assuming I don't have temperature in the model, the effect of vegetation density on the expected count will thus vary over time. If I wanted to model that, then I'd fit year-specific effects of vegetation cover or perhaps even visit-specific effects. And nowadays, for such a big batch of parameters, I'd normally make the random effects assumption for such effects.

But would I do this ? No, since I would consider this model too complex, unless I was specifically interested in exactly such effects.

I have often felt that from a biological point of view, if we think about things in a more mechanistic manner, then there is hardly anything in our models that can really, really be assumed a constant. So, we might want to make almost everything in our models random effects. But we don't and this is probably a good thing, since it would make our model far too complex and thus go against Occam's Razor.

Now, what do we treat as random and what do we treat as fixed ? That's the art of modeling .... or we let some machine learning magic decide based on cross-validation etc.

So, it is considerations like these which would let me start with an occupancy model that does not have site-level random intercepts in the linear predictor for p.
Best regards --- Marc
